passage: Six weeks to boards. Old me: an hour of running, then guilt about not studying, then studying badly because of the guilt. New thinking, written down so I'll remember it: movement isn't a rival of marks; it's part of how I stay sharp. I've noticed I remember chapters better after a walk. So the plan is twenty minutes at 5:30 every evening, fixed, not longer. After two hours of study, five minutes of stretching. That's it. No hour-long runs until boards are done. My sister Hafsa said she would join for the skipping. I don't feel I'm giving up sport. I feel like I've found the size of it that fits this season. — Seema

qa.q: How long are Seema's exercise sessions now?
qa.a: Twenty minutes, fixed at 5:30 every evening.

qa.q: How does Seema now feel about exercise during exams?
qa.a: Relieved and less guilty: the shorter fixed slots feel like the right size for this season.

qa.q: What else could Seema do on the heaviest study days, and why?
qa.a: Keep just a short walk instead of skipping movement completely, since even a little keeps the habit and clears the head.

qa.q: How does the plan look to Hafsa?
qa.a: Hafsa sees Seema still moving instead of giving up sport, and joining for the skipping lets Hafsa help without adding pressure.

grounding: A teen with board exams shortens exercise to twenty minutes in fixed slots, treating movement as a study aid.

subtopic: Reaching a fitness or sports goal

passage:
In their village near Margao, Maria used to play football on the church ground every evening for an hour and a half. With the Class Ten boards seven weeks away, her mother wanted her to stop completely.
Maria thought it through on the walk home. If I stop, I'll sit at the desk longer, but I already stare at the same page after dinner. If I play the full ninety minutes, I lose too much time. So what's in between?
She proposed it at dinner: twenty minutes, fixed, six to six-twenty, just passing drills with her cousin Sumit, then straight home to study. “It's not football against marks. It's so my head works.”
Her mother agreed to try it for two weeks.
By the end of the first week, Maria was finishing her evening maths set before nine, something she hadn't managed all month. Sumit complained that twenty minutes was too short. She didn't budge.

qa.a: Twenty minutes, six to six-twenty, passing drills with Sumit.

qa.q: How did Maria feel about stopping football completely?
qa.a: Maria was worried it wouldn't help, since sitting longer already meant staring at the same page, and felt determined to find something in between.

qa.q: What else could Maria try if twenty minutes gets hard to fit in near exams?
qa.a: Keep the same slot but make it a brisk walk or skipping, so the habit of a head-clearing break continues.

qa.q: How might Maria's mother see the two-week trial?
qa.a: She may start doubtful, but seeing the maths set finished before nine would likely reassure her.

grounding: Shows a teen with board exams reasoning her way to twenty-minute fixed football slots, using movement to help focus rather than competing with marks.
